lessons.title: Sign in to Codex and complete your first delegated task
lessons.summary: Install Codex, sign in with your ChatGPT account instead of an API key, and delegate a small, safe first task so you understand approval modes before touching real work.
lessons.goal: Get Codex installed, signed in with your ChatGPT plan, and complete one small, reviewed task.
lessons.whyItMatters: Codex is a coding agent, not just a chat window — it can read, edit, and run commands in your repository. Getting the sign-in method and approval mode right on day one avoids two common early mistakes: accidentally billing per-token on an API key instead of using your ChatGPT plan, and letting an agent make unreviewed changes to a real project before you trust it.
lessons.beforeYouStart: An active ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, or Enterprise plan (Free and Go tiers get little or no Codex access). A terminal with Node.js or Homebrew installed. A project folder to practice in — a scratch repo or a low-stakes personal project, not production code.
steps: Install the Codex CLI: `npm install -g @openai/codex` (or `brew install codex`).
Open a terminal in a project folder and run `codex`.
When prompted, choose 'Sign in with ChatGPT' rather than an API key — this draws usage from your existing plan allowance instead of billing per token.
Pick a conservative approval mode to start: read-only or 'suggest', so Codex proposes changes without writing files until you approve.
Give Codex one small, clearly bounded first task (see the prompt below).
Read the diff or explanation Codex produces before approving anything.
Approve, reject, or ask for a change — then check the usage indicator to see how much of your 5-hour window you used.
lessons.prompt: Add a new file called CONTRIBUTING.md to this repository. It should explain in 4-6 short bullet points: (1) this project currently has no build step, (2) how to run it locally, (3) where the main entry point is, (4) that PRs should include a one-line description of what changed. Do not modify or delete any existing files. Show me the exact content before you write it.
lessons.explanation: The prompt is deliberately narrow: one new file, explicit 'do not modify existing files' guardrail, and an instruction to show content before writing. This lets you evaluate Codex's judgment on something low-risk while you're still learning how it behaves. Signing in with your ChatGPT account (rather than an API key) matters because Codex usage is metered against your plan's rolling 5-hour window, shared across the CLI, web, and IDE extension — an API key instead bills per token against a separate developer account.
lessons.example: In an empty test repository, a developer runs `codex`, signs in with ChatGPT, selects suggest mode, and pastes the CONTRIBUTING.md prompt. Codex reads the repo structure, drafts the file content, and shows it before writing. The developer approves, and Codex creates exactly one new file — nothing else in the repo changes.
lessons.exercise: In your own ChatGPT/Codex account, install the CLI, sign in, and open a real repo you have access to. Ask Codex to explain (not edit) what one specific file does, in plain language with the file path cited. Then, in suggest mode, ask it to add one small, clearly non-destructive file like the CONTRIBUTING.md example above.
lessons.expectedResult: Codex signs in successfully and shows your plan/usage status. For the explanation task, it responds with an accurate, cited description. For the file task, it shows you the proposed content before anything is written, and only the one file you asked for is created.
commonMistakes: Signing in with an API key out of habit, then being surprised that usage is billed per token instead of coming from the ChatGPT plan allowance.
Starting in a full-access/auto-approve mode on a real or unfamiliar repository before learning how Codex behaves.
Giving a vague, multi-part first task ('clean up the repo') instead of one narrow, verifiable action.
lessons.proTip: Usage is metered in a rolling 5-hour window shared across the CLI, the web app, and the IDE extension — not per surface. If you're testing in more than one place, you're drawing from the same pool. Plus plans get roughly 15-80 messages per window depending on task size; if you run out, Codex Settings → Usage → Credits lets you buy more without upgrading your plan.

lessons.title: Use Codex to understand an unfamiliar repository before touching it
lessons.summary: Get Codex to build and explain an accurate map of a codebase's architecture, entry points, and one real request flow — before you write a single line.
lessons.goal: Produce a reliable, cited overview of an unfamiliar repository's structure and one key flow through it.
lessons.whyItMatters: Most real work with a coding agent starts inside a codebase someone else wrote — a client project, a job's existing repo, an open-source dependency. Codex can read an entire repository fast, but only if you ask it to explain with citations rather than summarize from a guess. Doing this exploration in read-only mode first, before any edit task, prevents changes based on a wrong mental model.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real repository you have access to — a work project or a cloned open-source repo. Codex CLI installed and signed in.
steps: Open the repo in a terminal and start `codex` in read-only mode — no edits at this stage.
Ask for a guided tour: what the project does, its entry point(s), and its top-level directory layout.
Ask it to trace one specific, real flow through the code (e.g. what happens when a user submits a form, or how a request is handled) file by file, citing paths.
Ask how tests are structured and what command actually runs them.
Check whether the repo already has an AGENTS.md file at the root.
If there is no AGENTS.md, ask Codex to draft one based only on what it found in the repo, for your review — do not accept it unread.
Save the summary somewhere your team can find it (README, wiki, ticket).
lessons.prompt:
You are in read-only mode. Do not edit any files. Give me:
1. A one-paragraph summary of what this project does.
2. The main entry point file(s), with paths.
3. The top-level directory structure and what each major folder is for.
4. A step-by-step trace of what happens when [describe one real flow, e.g. 'a user submits the checkout form'], citing the specific files and functions involved, in order.
5. The exact command(s) to run the test suite.
For anything you're not confident about, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
lessons.explanation: Asking for citations (specific file paths, in order) forces Codex to ground its answer in what it actually read rather than produce a plausible-sounding but generic summary. The explicit 'say so if not confident' instruction reduces confident-but-wrong answers on the parts of the codebase it's less certain about. Tracing one concrete flow end to end is more useful than a generic architecture description because it's directly checkable — you can open the cited files and verify.
lessons.example: A developer joins a project and points Codex at an unfamiliar Next.js e-commerce repo, asking it to trace what happens from checkout button click through to order confirmation. Codex responds with the client component that handles the click, the API route it calls, the database write, and the confirmation email trigger — each with a file path. The developer opens two of the cited files to spot-check accuracy before trusting the rest.
lessons.exercise: Pick a real repository you have access to (work or open source). In read-only mode, ask Codex for the guided tour and one traced flow using the prompt above. Open at least two of the file paths it cites yourself to confirm they say what Codex claims.
lessons.expectedResult: You get a structured overview with specific file paths you can verify, an accurate trace of one real flow, the correct test command, and an honest flag on anything Codex was unsure about rather than a confident guess.
commonMistakes: Trusting the summary without opening any of the cited files to check accuracy.
Asking Codex to explain and make changes in the same request, which mixes exploration with edits before you've verified the mental model.
Skipping the question about how tests run, then later not knowing how to verify any change Codex makes.
lessons.proTip: If the repo has no AGENTS.md, this exploration is the perfect moment to create one. Ask Codex to draft it from what it just found — build/test commands, key conventions, directories that are off-limits — then edit it yourself before committing. Every future Codex session in this repo will read that file automatically.

lessons.title: Write specifications Codex can implement without back-and-forth
lessons.summary: Learn the structure of a spec that gives Codex enough context, constraints, and a definition of done to implement correctly on the first pass.
lessons.goal: Write a task specification with enough context, constraints, and acceptance criteria that Codex implements it correctly with minimal clarification.
lessons.whyItMatters: The single biggest driver of good or bad output from a coding agent is the quality of the instruction it's given. A vague request ('add search to the app') forces Codex to guess at scope, data source, and UI — guesses that are expensive to unwind later. A tight spec turns a coding agent from a slot machine into a predictable tool, and the skill transfers directly to writing tickets for human developers too.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A real, small feature or fix you actually want built — pick something you could describe in under a minute if a colleague asked.
steps: State the goal in one sentence: what should exist when this is done, and why.
List acceptance criteria: specific, checkable statements ('user sees an error message if the field is empty'), not adjectives ('better UX').
List constraints and non-goals: what NOT to change, any tech/library restrictions, anything explicitly out of scope for this task.
Name the files or areas likely involved, if you know them — this narrows the search space.
State how success will be verified: which command to run, which test to pass, what to check manually.
Feed the spec to Codex and ask for a plan before implementation, not code directly.
Check the plan against your acceptance criteria before approving the implementation.
lessons.prompt:
Task: Add a CSV export button to the Orders table.

Goal: Users can download the currently filtered/visible orders as a CSV file.

Acceptance criteria:
- A button labeled 'Export CSV' appears above the orders table.
- Clicking it downloads a .csv file containing only the rows currently visible (respecting active filters), with the same columns shown in the table.
- If there are zero visible rows, the button is disabled with a tooltip 'No orders to export'.

Constraints:
- Do not change the filtering logic itself.
- Do not add a new backend endpoint — generate the CSV client-side from the data already loaded in the table.
- Do not modify any other page.

Likely files: src/components/OrdersTable.tsx and its existing column config.

Definition of done: `npm run test` passes, and a manual check confirms the downloaded file's rows match what's on screen.

Before implementing, show me your plan: which files you'll touch and how.
lessons.explanation: Each section closes off a category of ambiguity: the goal prevents scope confusion, acceptance criteria give Codex (and you) a checklist instead of vibes, constraints prevent well-intentioned scope creep (like adding a backend endpoint you didn't ask for), and the definition of done gives Codex a concrete way to verify its own work instead of declaring victory by assumption. Asking for a plan before code lets you catch a wrong approach while it's still cheap to redirect.
lessons.example: A team lead wants a rate limit added to a login endpoint. A vague version ('add rate limiting to login') risks Codex picking an arbitrary library, threshold, and error format. The spec version states the exact threshold (5 attempts / 15 minutes), the exact response (429 with a specific JSON error shape already used elsewhere in the API), and explicitly excludes touching any other endpoint — producing a implementation that matches what was actually needed on the first pass.
lessons.exercise: Pick one real, small feature or fix you want in a project of yours. Write a spec using the template above — goal, acceptance criteria, constraints, likely files, definition of done. Give it to Codex and ask for a plan first; compare the plan against your acceptance criteria before letting it implement anything.
lessons.expectedResult: Codex returns a plan that maps clearly onto your acceptance criteria and respects your stated constraints, with little or no need to re-explain the task.
commonMistakes: Writing acceptance criteria as adjectives ('clean', 'better', 'intuitive') instead of checkable statements.
Omitting constraints and non-goals, which lets the agent 'helpfully' touch unrelated code or add infrastructure you didn't want.
Skipping the definition of done, so there's no shared way to know when the task is actually finished.
lessons.proTip: A spec is task-specific; an AGENTS.md file is standing, repo-wide context (build commands, conventions, off-limits paths) that applies to every task. Keep them separate — put anything true for every future task in AGENTS.md so you stop repeating it in specs.

lessons.title: Delegate a full feature implementation with review checkpoints
lessons.summary: Run a complete implementation cycle with Codex — plan, implement, self-test, and diff review — for a bounded feature, using checkpoints instead of blind auto-approval.
lessons.goal: Have Codex implement a real, bounded feature end-to-end, with a plan you approve first and a diff you review before merging.
lessons.whyItMatters: This is the core workflow professional Codex use is built on: not one-shot magic, but a structured loop of plan → implement → verify → review that keeps a human in control of what actually ships. Doing this well is what separates 'Codex saved me an afternoon' from 'Codex quietly broke something in production.'
lessons.beforeYouStart: A repository with an existing test suite. Ideally an AGENTS.md at the root (see the previous lessons) so Codex already knows build/test commands and conventions.
steps: Write the feature as a spec: goal, acceptance criteria, constraints, definition of done (use the template from the previous lesson).
Start Codex and ask for an implementation plan before any code is written.
Review the plan: does it match your acceptance criteria, and does it avoid touching things you excluded?
Approve the plan, or send it back with specific corrections.
Let Codex implement, then explicitly ask it to run the test suite and show you the actual output.
Review the diff file by file — not just the summary — checking it against your acceptance criteria.
Ask for targeted changes if anything is off, rather than re-describing the whole task.
Approve and commit only once the diff, the test output, and your criteria all line up.
lessons.prompt:
Task: Add rate limiting to the /api/login endpoint.

Acceptance criteria:
- More than 5 failed login attempts from the same IP within 15 minutes returns HTTP 429 with body { "error": "too_many_attempts" }.
- Successful logins do not count toward the limit.
- The limit resets after the 15-minute window.

Constraints: only touch the login route and its middleware. Do not add a new database table — use the existing Redis client already configured in src/lib/redis.ts.

Definition of done: `npm test` passes, including a new test for the 429 case, and existing login tests still pass unmodified.

First, give me your implementation plan: which files you'll create or change and why. Wait for my approval before writing any code. Once approved, implement it, then run the full test suite and paste the exact output.
lessons.explanation: The plan-first checkpoint catches a wrong architectural choice (e.g. a new database table when a constraint forbids it) before any code exists, which is far cheaper to fix than after implementation. Explicitly requiring the actual test output — not a claim that tests pass — closes the gap between 'Codex says it works' and 'it demonstrably works.' Reviewing the diff file by file against your original acceptance criteria is the final human checkpoint before the change ships.
lessons.example: A developer gives Codex the rate-limiting spec above. Codex's plan proposes a small middleware function reading from the existing Redis client, plus one new test file — matching the constraint against a new database table. The developer approves, Codex implements it, runs `npm test`, and pastes output showing 34 passing tests including the new 429 case. The developer reviews the diff (12 lines in the middleware, 18 in the new test) and merges.
lessons.exercise: Take the spec you wrote in the previous lesson (or write a new small one) and run it through this full plan → implement → test → review cycle in your own repo. Do not skip the plan-approval step even if you're confident about what you want.
lessons.expectedResult: You get an approved plan that matches your constraints, an implementation with real (pasted) test output confirming it works, and a diff small and clear enough to review line by line before merging.
commonMistakes: Switching to full auto-approve for the first real feature task instead of keeping the plan and diff checkpoints.
Accepting 'tests pass' as a claim instead of asking for the actual command output.
Giving one large, multi-feature task instead of splitting it into smaller, independently reviewable pieces.
lessons.proTip: For a genuinely hard or ambiguous task, ask Codex to try more than one approach and compare trade-offs before you pick one to implement fully (its best-of-N generation mode is built for exactly this) — cheaper than discovering the wrong approach after a full implementation.

lessons.title: Debug a failing build or test with Codex, without guessing
lessons.summary: Use Codex to reproduce, diagnose, and fix a failing build or test with a real root cause, instead of accepting the first plausible-looking patch.
lessons.goal: Fix a failing build or test with a verified root cause and a minimal diff, confirmed by a full rerun of the suite.
lessons.whyItMatters: A coding agent under pressure to 'just make it pass' will sometimes take the fastest route — loosening an assertion, adding a try/catch that swallows the error, or skipping the failing test. That fixes the symptom, not the bug, and it can quietly reintroduce the same failure later. Teaching Codex to reproduce first and explain the root cause before patching keeps fixes honest.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A repository with a currently failing build or test, and the full error output/stack trace from your CI or local run — not just the summary line.
steps: Paste the complete error output and stack trace, not a paraphrase.
Ask Codex to reproduce the failure locally first, and confirm it sees the same error before proposing any fix.
Ask for a root-cause hypothesis, stated in plain language, before any code changes.
Ask what evidence supports that hypothesis (which line, which condition, which input).
Only after the hypothesis is confirmed, ask for the minimal fix.
Explicitly ask whether the fix touches any existing test, and if so, why.
Rerun the entire test suite, not just the previously failing test, and review the full output.
lessons.prompt:
Here is the exact failing test output:

[PASTE FULL ERROR OUTPUT AND STACK TRACE]

First, reproduce this locally and confirm you see the same failure — show me the command and output. Then explain your root-cause hypothesis in plain language, citing the specific line(s) responsible. Do not propose a fix yet. Once I confirm your hypothesis makes sense, implement the minimal fix. Tell me explicitly if the fix requires changing any existing test, and if so, explain exactly why the old test's expectation was wrong. Finally, run the full test suite (not just this test) and paste the complete output.
lessons.explanation: Requiring reproduction before diagnosis rules out fixes based on a misread of the stack trace. Requiring the hypothesis to be stated and justified before any code is touched creates a checkpoint where you can say 'that's not actually the cause, look closer' before wasted effort goes into the wrong fix. Explicitly flagging test modifications surfaces the riskiest kind of 'fix' — one that makes the failure disappear by changing what correctness means, rather than by correcting the code.
lessons.example: A CI run fails with a TypeError in a date-formatting function when a null value is passed. Codex reproduces it locally, identifies that a recent change removed a null check upstream, and proposes restoring the check at the actual source of the null rather than adding a defensive try/catch inside the formatter. It confirms no existing test needed modification, then reruns the full suite showing all 210 tests passing.
lessons.exercise: Find (or intentionally cause) a failing test or build in a practice repo. Run it through this reproduce → hypothesize → fix → full-rerun cycle using the prompt above, and pay particular attention to whether Codex ever proposes touching an existing test.
lessons.expectedResult: You get a confirmed root cause backed by specific evidence, a minimal fix that addresses that cause, an honest answer about whether any existing test changed, and a full test suite run (not just the one test) showing everything passing.
commonMistakes: Pasting only the error message instead of the full stack trace, which forces Codex to guess at context it actually needs.
Accepting the first proposed fix without confirming the root-cause hypothesis first.
Letting the fix quietly skip, loosen, or delete the failing test instead of fixing the underlying code.
lessons.proTip: If a fix does legitimately require changing a test (the test itself encoded wrong behavior), ask Codex to explain the old expectation, the new expectation, and why the change is correct — in the commit message, not just in chat — so the reasoning survives for the next reviewer.

lessons.title: Use Codex code review without rubber-stamping it
lessons.summary: Turn on automated Codex review on your pull requests and use the CLI for on-demand diff review, while keeping the judgment about which comments matter with a human.
lessons.goal: Get useful, targeted review comments from Codex on a real pull request, and correctly triage which ones to act on.
lessons.whyItMatters: Codex can review every pull request automatically and comment on GitHub, which is genuinely useful for catching bugs a rushed human review misses — but it's a second opinion, not a verdict. Teams that treat every Codex comment as mandatory either drown in noise or, worse, learn to ignore the tool entirely. The skill is judgment: which comments to act on, which to dismiss with a reason, and when to ask it to review again after changes.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A GitHub repository you can configure, or at least open pull requests in. Codex CLI signed in for the on-demand diff review step.
steps: Enable Codex code review on the repository (via the Codex GitHub integration) so it comments automatically on new PRs.
Open or pick a real pull request and read its automatic review comments.
For any diff not yet in a PR, use the CLI directly and ask Codex to review the current diff before you even open one.
For each comment, decide: fix it, or reject it with a one-line reason (e.g. 'intentional, see ticket #123').
Don't let review comments block on style preferences already enforced by your linter/formatter — tell Codex to skip those.
After addressing real issues, ask for a second pass on just the changed lines rather than the whole PR again.
Use the pattern of comments over time to inform what you add to AGENTS.md (e.g. if it keeps flagging the same convention, document the convention explicitly).
lessons.prompt: Review the current diff for correctness bugs, security issues, and missed edge cases only — do not comment on style or formatting already enforced by the project's linter. For each issue you find: cite the exact file and line, explain concretely why it's a problem (not just 'this could be improved'), and suggest a minimal fix. If you're not sure something is actually a bug, say so explicitly instead of stating it as fact.
lessons.explanation: Scoping the review to correctness, security, and edge cases (and explicitly excluding style) keeps the output focused on things worth a human's attention instead of noise a linter already handles. Requiring a concrete 'why' per comment, not just a flag, is what lets you triage quickly — you can evaluate the reasoning instead of re-deriving whether the comment is right. The 'say so if unsure' instruction matters because unreviewed acceptance of a confidently-wrong review comment is its own failure mode.
lessons.example: On a PR adding a payment webhook handler, Codex's review flags that the handler doesn't verify the webhook signature before processing the payload — citing the exact line where the raw body is parsed — and suggests adding the signature check used elsewhere in the codebase. The team fixes it. A second, lower-confidence comment about variable naming is dismissed as a style preference already covered by the linter.
lessons.exercise: On a real pull request (yours or a practice one), turn on or manually run Codex review using the prompt above. Go through every comment and explicitly decide fix or reject-with-reason for each one — don't leave any unaddressed.
lessons.expectedResult: You get a short list of specific, cited comments focused on real risk, and you can explain your reasoning for accepting or rejecting each one rather than accepting or ignoring the whole batch by default.
commonMistakes: Treating every Codex review comment as mandatory and fixing things that don't actually matter, training the team to dread PRs.
Using Codex as the only reviewer with no human sign-off on a meaningful change.
Asking for a review before the code even runs or passes tests, producing comments about code that's about to change anyway.
lessons.proTip: New team members especially should be taught to read Codex review comments critically, not as instructions — ask them to write one sentence justifying whether they agree with each comment before applying it. That habit is worth more long-term than any individual fix.

lessons.title: Build a landing page from a spec, without touching code yourself
lessons.summary: Turn a real page brief — an open house, a promotion, a service offer — into a working, mobile-responsive landing page by writing a tight content-and-constraints spec and letting Codex build it.
lessons.goal: Get Codex to build a working, correct, mobile-responsive single-page site from your own content, without inventing facts or over-engineering the build.
lessons.whyItMatters: A landing page for a listing, a promotion, or a service is one of the most common small projects a non-developer professional needs — and hiring a developer or wrestling with a website builder for a single page is often overkill. Codex can build a clean, correct static page directly from a written brief, but only if the brief supplies real content and explicit constraints; left vague, it will either invent details you didn't provide or build far more infrastructure than a one-page site needs.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A folder on your computer for the project, and Codex CLI installed and signed in (if you're not comfortable with a terminal, a developer or technical colleague can run this step for you using your spec — the spec itself is the deliverable either way). Have your actual content ready: headline, key details, contact information, and any photos or logos as files.
steps: Gather your real content first: headline, subheading, the sections you want, exact contact details (phone, email, address), and your call to action. Do not let Codex invent any of this.
Write the spec: page goal, sections in order, required elements, tone/style direction, and a hard technical constraint that it must be a simple static page (HTML/CSS/JS, no backend, no database).
State the definition of done: opens correctly in a browser, looks correct and usable at mobile width, and contains no content you didn't provide.
Start Codex in an empty project folder and give it the spec, asking for a short plan first.
Check the plan for sanity — if it proposes a framework, backend, or database for a one-page brief, redirect it back to 'static HTML/CSS/JS only.'
Approve implementation, then open the resulting page in your browser to preview it.
Resize your browser window (or use your browser's device toolbar) to check the layout at mobile width.
Request specific revisions as small, precise notes ('make the phone number larger and put it in the header') rather than vague feedback ('make it better').
lessons.prompt:
Build a single static landing page for a real estate open house.

Content (use exactly this, do not add or invent anything):
- Headline: "Open House: 123 Maple St, Saturday 1-4 PM"
- Subheading: "3 bed / 2 bath, 1,850 sq ft, newly renovated kitchen"
- Sections in order: (1) Hero with headline, subheading, and a large 'RSVP' button, (2) a photo gallery placeholder grid (4 images, use styled placeholder boxes since I'll add real photos later), (3) a short "About this home" paragraph: [PASTE 2-3 SENTENCES], (4) a contact section with agent name "[NAME]", phone "[PHONE]", email "[EMAIL]".
- CTA: the RSVP button should be a mailto: link to [EMAIL] with subject line "Open House RSVP".

Style: clean and professional, mobile-first, generous white space, one accent color (navy blue). No stock photography, no invented testimonials, no invented pricing.

Technical constraints: a single static page — plain HTML, CSS, and vanilla JS only. No frameworks, no build step, no backend, no database. It must open directly in a browser from the file.

Definition of done: opens correctly as a local file, looks correct and usable at a 375px-wide mobile viewport, and contains only the content listed above.

First give me a short plan (what files you'll create), then implement it.
lessons.explanation: Supplying the literal content in the spec (headline, contact details, exact CTA behavior) is what prevents Codex from inventing a phone number, a price, or a testimonial that doesn't exist — a real risk with an under-specified brief. The explicit 'static HTML/CSS/JS only, no framework, no backend' constraint keeps the build proportional to a one-page brief instead of scaffolding infrastructure you don't need and can't maintain. Stating the mobile-width check as part of the definition of done matters because most visitors to a page like this will open it on a phone.
lessons.example: Maria, a real estate agent, has an open house this Saturday and no time to brief a designer. She fills in the spec above with her listing's real headline, a two-sentence property description, and her own phone/email, and runs it through Codex. In a few minutes she has an index.html and styles.css that open correctly in her browser: a clean hero section with her exact headline, a photo placeholder grid she can swap in real listing photos for later, and an RSVP button that opens her email client with the subject line pre-filled. She resizes her browser to check it on a simulated phone width, asks for one revision — a larger phone number in the header — and it's ready to send to her broker to host.
lessons.exercise: Pick a real page you actually need (an open house, a local promotion, a one-page pitch for your freelance services) and fill in the spec template above with your real content and contact details. Run it through Codex in your own account, open the resulting page in your browser, and resize the window to check it at mobile width.
lessons.expectedResult: A working static page that opens directly in a browser, contains only the content you supplied (no invented facts, prices, or testimonials), reads and functions correctly at mobile width, and has all required elements — CTA and contact info — present and accurate.
commonMistakes: Giving a one-line prompt ('make me a landing page for my listing') and getting generic or fabricated content because no real content was supplied.
Not specifying 'static only, no backend' and getting back an over-engineered setup with a framework and database for what should be one HTML file.
Approving the page without checking it at mobile width, where most real visitors will actually view it.
Accepting placeholder content (fake testimonials, sample pricing) as if it were real and publishing it as-is.
lessons.proTip: Keep your real copy in a separate short content file (content.md) instead of retyping it into every prompt. When you need a revision, edit content.md and ask Codex to 're-apply the page to match this updated content' — faster and less error-prone than rewriting the whole spec each time.

lessons.title: Choose between local Codex sessions and parallel cloud tasks
lessons.summary: Understand when to run Codex locally versus as a background cloud task against a connected GitHub repo, and how to run several bounded tasks in parallel without losing control of quality.
lessons.goal: Correctly choose local vs. cloud Codex for a given task, and run multiple well-specified cloud tasks in parallel safely.
lessons.whyItMatters: Codex Cloud lets you fire off several tasks at once against a connected GitHub repository, each running in its own isolated sandbox and returning a pull request — a real productivity multiplier for well-bounded work. But cloud tasks run unsupervised: ambiguity that a local session would let you catch mid-task instead compounds silently until you're looking at a finished PR. Knowing which tasks belong where is what makes parallelism safe rather than reckless.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A GitHub repository connected at chatgpt.com/codex, and comfort with the spec-writing workflow from earlier lessons — cloud tasks depend on it even more than local ones.
steps: Default to local CLI sessions for anything you need to iterate on closely: exploratory debugging, tasks where you'll want to interrupt and redirect, or anything touching code you don't fully trust yet.

Reserve cloud tasks for work that's well-specified, bounded, and lower-stakes to get slightly wrong on the first pass — dependency bumps, adding tests to an already-understood module, a described bug fix.
At chatgpt.com/codex, connect the target GitHub repo if it isn't already connected.
Write each cloud task as a full spec (goal, constraints, definition of done) exactly as you would for a local session — there's no one present to clarify a vague instruction.
Fire off multiple independent, non-overlapping tasks in parallel rather than one at a time.
Review the resulting pull requests, not code-in-progress — cloud tasks aren't meant to be watched live.
Pull any promising PR down locally and run the full test suite yourself before merging (see the next lesson).
Monitor and manage running tasks from the desktop or iOS app if you're away from your main machine.
lessons.prompt:
Cloud task: Upgrade the ESLint config to the latest recommended ruleset and fix all resulting lint errors.

Constraints:
- Do not change any business logic — only formatting/lint-driven changes.
- Do not touch files under src/legacy/ — that directory is excluded from linting intentionally.
- If a rule violation requires a non-trivial logic change to fix (not just a mechanical fix), leave it with an eslint-disable comment and a TODO explaining why, rather than changing behavior.

Definition of done: `npm run lint` passes with zero errors, `npm test` still passes unchanged, and the PR description lists every file touched and why.
lessons.explanation: The constraints do more work here than in a local session, because there's no back-and-forth to catch an overreach mid-task — the 'no business logic changes' and 'leave a TODO instead of guessing' instructions are what keep an unsupervised task from making a judgment call you'd have vetoed live. Writing the PR-description requirement into the spec turns the returned pull request itself into a reviewable artifact instead of a mystery diff.
lessons.example: A team fires three cloud tasks in parallel on a Friday afternoon: an ESLint upgrade (above), adding unit tests to a payment-calculation module that's already well understood, and a dependency bump with a changelog summary. By Monday, three PRs are waiting. The lint and dependency PRs merge after a quick review; the test-addition PR gets sent back once with a note that two of the new tests didn't actually assert anything meaningful.
lessons.exercise: Pick one real, well-bounded task in your own repo — a lint/format upgrade, a dependency bump, or adding tests to a module you already understand well. Write it as a full spec, run it as a cloud task at chatgpt.com/codex, and review the resulting PR without running any code live.
lessons.expectedResult: A pull request appears with a description matching your definition of done, changes scoped exactly to what you specified, and no surprises outside the stated constraints.
commonMistakes: Sending a vague or large task to the cloud where nobody is present to catch ambiguity compounding over the run.
Merging a cloud-produced PR straight from the GitHub UI without pulling it locally to run the full suite yourself.
Firing many cloud tasks in parallel without remembering that cloud usage draws from the same shared 5-hour window as your local CLI and IDE sessions.
lessons.proTip: Cloud tasks are best for work you'd be comfortable delegating to a competent contractor with a written brief and no further questions allowed — if you can't imagine handing the same spec to a person and getting the right result back, don't send it to the cloud yet.

lessons.title: Build real verification habits instead of trusting 'it works'
lessons.summary: Establish repeatable checks — real command output, test coverage for new code, and manual verification for what Codex can't see — so 'done' means demonstrated, not claimed.
lessons.goal: Replace 'Codex says it works' with a repeatable verification habit backed by actual command output and, where relevant, manual checks.
lessons.whyItMatters: A coding agent's claim that something works is a hypothesis, not proof — and under pressure to finish a task, it can be tempted toward the same shortcuts a rushed human would take: a loosened assertion, a skipped test, a change that looks plausible but was never actually run. The professionals who get consistently reliable results from Codex are the ones who never accept a claim of success without seeing the evidence themselves.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A repository with a test suite and a build/lint command you can name exactly (this pairs directly with what belongs in AGENTS.md).
steps: Never accept 'the tests pass' as a sentence — always require the actual command and its output.
For new functionality, ask Codex to write or extend tests as part of the task, not as an afterthought you request separately.
Explicitly ask whether any existing test was modified, and if so, require a plain-language justification for the change.
For anything Codex can't literally verify itself — visual layout, real third-party API behavior, cross-browser rendering — build a short manual verification checklist and run it yourself.
Rerun the full test suite before accepting a change, not just the tests related to the new code.
Maintain a 'definition of done' checklist consistent with what's in AGENTS.md so this isn't reinvented per task.
Add anything you had to verify by hand more than once to a documented, repeatable checklist for next time.
lessons.prompt:
Before you tell me this task is complete:
1. Run the exact test command (`npm test`) and paste the full output, not a summary.
2. Run the exact build command (`npm run build`) and paste the full output.
3. Tell me explicitly: did you add or modify any test files? List them and explain why for each.
4. List anything in this change that you could not verify yourself (e.g. visual appearance, behavior of an external API, anything requiring a running browser) so I can check it manually.
Do not summarize results as 'all passing' — show the actual output.
lessons.explanation: Requiring pasted output rather than a summary closes the gap between claim and evidence — a summary can be wrong or optimistic in a way that raw output rarely is. The explicit question about modified tests surfaces the specific failure mode where a suite goes green because an assertion was weakened rather than because the code got fixed. The 'what couldn't you verify' question is what catches the blind spots inherent to an agent that can run commands but can't see a rendered page or a real third-party response the way a human tester can.
lessons.example: A developer asks Codex to add a discount-calculation feature. Codex reports test and build output showing everything green, confirms it added three new tests and modified none, and flags that it could not verify how the discount badge actually renders on the checkout page since that requires a running browser. The developer opens the app locally, checks the badge renders correctly at both desktop and mobile width, and only then merges.
lessons.exercise: On a real task in your own repo, use the verification prompt above and read the full pasted output rather than skimming for 'passed.' If Codex flags anything it couldn't verify itself, check it manually before accepting the change.
lessons.expectedResult: You have actual command output confirming the build and test suite pass, a clear answer on whether any existing test changed and why, and a short, explicit list of anything you personally need to check by hand — checked before merging.
commonMistakes: Accepting a written claim that tests pass without ever seeing the command output.
Not noticing that an existing test's assertion was quietly loosened or the test was skipped to make the suite go green.
Skipping manual verification entirely for anything Codex flags it couldn't check itself, especially UI and visual behavior.
lessons.proTip: Put your exact test, build, and lint commands directly in AGENTS.md under a 'Verification' heading. When Codex always knows the real commands to run, you stop getting plausible-sounding but wrong guesses at how to check its own work.

lessons.title: Run a complete delivery workflow: spec to merged PR
lessons.summary: Combine spec-writing, local or cloud implementation, verification, and code review into one repeatable delivery pipeline with clear human checkpoints from ticket to merge.
lessons.goal: Take a real task from a written spec through implementation, verification, and review to a merged pull request, with deliberate human checkpoints at each stage.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every earlier lesson in this path is a piece; this is the assembly. Professionals who get durable value from Codex don't treat each session as a one-off — they run the same repeatable pipeline every time, so quality doesn't depend on how careful they happened to feel that day. This is also where AGENTS.md earns its keep: a living document that gets better every time the pipeline surfaces something worth remembering.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A repository with tests, GitHub-based PRs, and ideally Codex code review enabled. Comfort with the spec template, verification habits, and review triage from earlier lessons in this path.
steps: Turn the task (bug, ticket, feature request) into a full spec: goal, acceptance criteria, constraints, definition of done.
Decide local CLI or cloud task based on how bounded and well-understood the work is.
Implement with checkpoints: approve the plan before code, review the diff before accepting.
Require Codex to run the real build/test/lint commands and paste actual output — never accept a claim.
Open the pull request with a description that states what changed and why, matching the spec's acceptance criteria.
Let automated Codex review comment on the PR; triage every comment as fix or reject-with-reason.
Do a final human read of the complete diff and PR description yourself, even if every earlier checkpoint looked fine.
Merge, then verify the change in the real running environment, not just in test output.
Ask: did anything here reveal a convention or command Codex should have already known? If so, add it to AGENTS.md before moving on.
lessons.prompt:
Ticket: [PASTE TICKET TITLE AND DESCRIPTION]

Write this as a full spec (goal, acceptance criteria, constraints, definition of done) and show it to me before implementing anything.

Once I approve the spec: give me your implementation plan first. Once I approve the plan: implement it, then run the full test suite, the build, and the linter, and paste the complete output of each. Tell me explicitly whether any existing test was modified and why. Then draft a pull request description stating exactly what changed and how it satisfies each acceptance criterion, so I can open the PR myself.
lessons.explanation: Chaining the checkpoints explicitly — spec approval, then plan approval, then verified implementation, then a PR description mapped back to acceptance criteria — means no single stage has to bear all the responsibility for catching a problem. Asking Codex to draft the PR description itself, tied to the acceptance criteria, produces a reviewable artifact for the next person (a teammate, a future you) rather than a diff with no explanation of intent.
lessons.example: A support ticket describes a bug where discount codes stack incorrectly at checkout. A developer turns it into a spec with the exact expected calculation, runs it locally with plan and diff checkpoints, gets pasted test/build/lint output, opens the PR with a description Codex drafted mapping the fix to the ticket's acceptance criteria, triages two Codex review comments (one fixed, one rejected as a pre-existing pattern used elsewhere), does a final read of the 40-line diff herself, and merges. Afterward she adds one line to AGENTS.md: 'discount stacking rules live in src/pricing/discounts.ts — see that file before touching pricing logic.'
lessons.exercise: Take one real ticket or task in your own project and run it through this entire pipeline start to finish: spec, plan approval, implementation with real verification output, PR description, review triage, and a final personal read of the diff before merging. Afterward, write one sentence for AGENTS.md capturing anything you had to explain that Codex should already have known.
lessons.expectedResult: A merged pull request whose description accurately reflects the change, backed by real verification output at each stage, with every automated review comment explicitly triaged rather than ignored or blindly applied — and at least one concrete addition to AGENTS.md from what you learned.
commonMistakes: Skipping the final personal read of the full diff because every earlier automated checkpoint looked fine.
Merging a cloud-produced PR straight away without pulling it locally to rerun the full suite yourself.
Never updating AGENTS.md, so the same context has to be re-explained in every future task.
lessons.proTip: Treat AGENTS.md as a living document, not a one-time setup file. After each delivery, spend sixty seconds asking: did Codex get anything wrong or ask something that a single line in AGENTS.md would have prevented? That habit compounds — six months in, a well-maintained AGENTS.md is often the single biggest driver of first-pass accuracy on a repo.
